questionText: What are Queue<T> and Stack<T>, and when should you use each?
shortAnswer: Queue<T> is FIFO (enqueue/dequeue) for work pipelines and BFS; Stack<T> is LIFO (push/pop) for undo, expression evaluation, and DFS. Both are O(1) single-ended operations; neither supports efficient middle access or concurrent use (see concurrent collections).
detailedAnswer: Queue<T> models lines: Enqueue adds at the tail, Dequeue removes from the head, Peek inspects without removing, and Count reports length. Use it for task pipelines, message buffering, BFS traversal, and print/job spooling. Stack<T> models piles: Push/Pop/Peek at one end — undo stacks, bracket matching, expression evaluation (shunting-yard), syntax parsing, and iterative DFS (which avoids recursion depth limits). Both are thin wrappers over arrays (Queue<T> is a ring buffer; Stack<T> a growing array), so indexed access is absent by design — elementAt(i) would defeat the abstraction (use List<T> for random access). Clearing keeps capacity (Clear resets head/tail, buffer retained). TrimExcess exists on neither — recreate if the buffer must shrink. Neither is thread-safe: one producer + one consumer still races on head/tail (use ConcurrentQueue<T> or Channel<T>). ToArray/ToList snapshot for debugging; enumerating yields head-to-tail (queue) or top-to-bottom (stack) order without dequeuing.
internalWorking: Queue<T> is a circular array with head/tail indices wrapping modulo capacity; growth doubles and re-linearizes. Stack<T> is an array with a size pointer; Push writes at size++, Pop reads at --size. Both amortize to O(1); enumeration walks indices without mutating state.
realWorldUsage: Background job buffers, BFS over org charts/graphs, browser-history back stacks, undo in editors, and delimiter validation in parsers.
commonMistake: Dequeue/Pop on empty collections (InvalidOperationException — guard with Count or TryDequeue/TryPop), using List<T> as a queue (O(n) RemoveAt(0)), and sharing Queue<T> across threads without synchronization.
technicalConversation: Ask what happens when two threads share one Queue<T> — torn head/tail updates corrupt state silently (no exception), which is why the concurrent variants exist.
interviewFollowUp: How would you implement a queue using two stacks, and what is the amortized cost?
keyTakeaway: Queue = FIFO pipelines, Stack = LIFO nesting. Ring/array backed, O(1) ends, never shared across threads.

questionText: Why is List<T>.RemoveAt(0) a bad queue, and what should you use instead?
shortAnswer: RemoveAt(0) shifts every element left — O(n) per dequeue, O(n²) to drain. Queue<T>'s ring buffer dequeues in O(1). For concurrent producers/consumers use ConcurrentQueue<T> or Channel<T>; for capacity-bounded flows use BlockingCollection<T> or bounded channels.
detailedAnswer: List<T> stores elements contiguously, so removing the head memmoves n−1 items on every call. Draining 100k items costs ~5 billion element copies — visible as CPU in any profile. Queue<T> avoids this with head/tail cursors over a circular buffer: dequeue just advances head (O(1)), and growth doubles only on wrap exhaustion. Selection guide: single-threaded buffer → Queue<T>; multi-producer/consumer → ConcurrentQueue<T> (lock-free Treiber-style segments) or better Channel<T> (async-aware, backpressure, cancellation); bounded blocking handoff with take semantics → BlockingCollection<T> (or bounded Channel); priority ordering → PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>; double-ended needs → LinkedList<T> or a deque over two stacks (no BCL deque — a known gap). Peek/TryPeek let consumers inspect without committing. Count is O(1) everywhere here (maintained, not computed). For high-throughput pipelines, batching dequeues (drain up to N per iteration) amortizes synchronization and improves cache behavior.
internalWorking: RemoveAt(0) lowers to memmove of (count−1) * sizeof(T) bytes per call. Queue<T>.TryDequeue advances _head = (_head + 1) % array.Length — a few instructions, no copies. ConcurrentQueue segments the buffer (per-core lists) to avoid head/tail contention; Channel adds async waiter queues + completion semantics on top.
realWorldUsage: Log drains, socket read loops, task schedulers, BFS frontiers, and producer/consumer bridges between I/O and CPU stages.
commonMistake: Queue<T> shared across threads (silent corruption), unbounded queue growth under load spikes (add bounds), and polling TryDequeue in a tight loop (spin-wait CPU — use blocking take or async reads).
technicalConversation: Ask how they would bound memory when producers outpace consumers — bounded channels with Wait/DropOldest policies turn an OOM risk into a design decision.
interviewFollowUp: What does TryDequeue return when empty, and why is that pattern safer than Count-then-Dequeue?
keyTakeaway: Never dequeue from a List head. Ring buffers for single-threaded, channels for concurrent, bounds for safety.

questionText: What is PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority> and how do you use it?
shortAnswer: PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority> (.NET 6+) is a min-heap: Enqueue(element, priority) and Dequeue always returns the lowest-priority item in O(log n). Perfect for schedulers, Dijkstra/A*, merge flows, and top-K problems.
detailedAnswer: Before .NET 6 you hand-rolled heaps or abused SortedSet (O(log n) but unique-only and slower). PriorityQueue gives: Enqueue(element, priority), Dequeue (min first), Peek, TryDequeue/TryPeek (empty-safe), EnqueueDequeue (push then pop in one pass — ideal for bounded top-K), Count, Clear, and UnorderedItems for inspection. Priorities need not be unique; ties dequeue in FIFO-ish order only if you encode sequence into the priority (e.g. (priority, seq) tuples with a comparer). Custom ordering via IComparer<TPriority> (max-heap = reversed comparer). Complexities: enqueue/dequeue O(log n), peek O(1), Clear O(1) logically. Not thread-safe and not stable by default — wrap or sequence-stamp for concurrent/ordered needs. A* / Dijkstra: push (node, fScore), skip stale entries via a best-known dictionary (lazy deletion beats decrease-key, which the API lacks). Scheduling: timers keyed by due-time; merge K sorted streams by pushing heads. UnorderedItems + LINQ is fine for diagnostics, never for ordering guarantees.
internalWorking: Binary heap in an array: parent at (i−1)/2, children at 2i+1/2i+2. Enqueue bubbles up, Dequeue moves the last element to the root and sifts down — O(log n) swaps. Growth doubles the array like List<T>. No decrease-key API: stale entries + skip-on-pop is the idiomatic workaround.
realWorldUsage: Task schedulers, timer wheels, pathfinding, Huffman coding, event simulation, and leaderboard trims.
commonMistake: Assuming stability (equal priorities pop in arbitrary order — stamp sequences), using it across threads, and Dequeue on empty (throws — use TryDequeue).
technicalConversation: Ask how they would implement decrease-key for Dijkstra — the lazy-deletion pattern (push updated entry, skip stale pops via best-known map) is the working answer.
interviewFollowUp: How do you turn it into a max-heap, and what does EnqueueDequeue buy you for top-K?
keyTakeaway: Min-heap with O(log n) ops. Stamp sequences for stability; lazy-delete for decrease-key.

questionText: How do you validate nested delimiters with a stack, and what edge cases matter?
shortAnswer: Push opening brackets, pop on closers and require a match; leftovers or mismatches mean invalid. Edge cases: empty input (valid), interleaved types ([)], escaped/quoted delimiters, and huge inputs (iterative stack avoids recursion limits — the point of the exercise).
detailedAnswer: The algorithm: iterate chars; on opener ({[( push it (with position for error messages); on closer, the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opener, else invalid; at end, an empty stack means balanced. Positions turn boolean answers into diagnostics ('Mismatched ] at index 42, expected )'). Extend to quotes/escapes with a small state machine (in-string flag, backslash skip) — real parsers (JSON, compilers) layer lexing before bracket matching. Why iterative: recursive descent re-does this with the call stack, risking StackOverflow on adversarial nesting (10k+ deep JSON); the explicit Stack<T> version handles arbitrary depth bounded only by memory. Complexity O(n) time, O(depth) space. Variants: HTML tag matching (push tag names, self-closing tags ignored), undo systems (push inverse commands, pop to revert — Command pattern), and DFS (push neighbors, pop to backtrack — recursion simulated). Testing: property-style — random bracket strings validated against a reference, plus fuzzing with quotes/escapes.
internalWorking: Each push/pop is O(1) amortized array ops; the stack holds at most the nesting depth. No recursion means no 1MB-default-stack risk — depth is heap-bound (millions feasible).
realWorldUsage: Config/JSON pre-validation, template engines, compiler front-ends, undo buffers, backtracking search, and interview screens (still!).
commonMistake: Forgetting the empty-stack pop guard (exception instead of false), ignoring interleaving ([) ]), and recursive solutions that StackOverflow on deep input.
technicalConversation: Ask how they would report WHERE the mismatch is — positions on the stack turn a bool into a diagnostic, which is the production-vs-exercise gap.
interviewFollowUp: How does this generalize to undo/redo, and what extra state does redo require?
keyTakeaway: Push openers, match closers, empty at end. Track positions for errors; iterate, never recurse, for depth safety.

questionText: How do you design a bounded in-memory buffer for a fast producer and slow consumer?
shortAnswer: Bound the queue (capacity + overflow policy), make the handoff blocking or async, batch the drain, and expose depth metrics. In modern .NET: Channel<T>.CreateBounded with Wait/Drop policies — it encodes all four decisions in one API.
detailedAnswer: Unbounded buffers under load spikes are OOMs in disguise. The four decisions: (1) Bound: fixed capacity sized from memory budget (capacity × item size) and latency tolerance. (2) Overflow policy: block/wait (backpressure — slows producer, safest), drop-newest (telemetry), drop-oldest (keep fresh — dashboards), or grow-then-shed (hybrid). (3) Handoff: blocking take (dedicated consumer thread), async reads (await reader.WaitToReadAsync — no thread burned), or polling with backoff (last resort). (4) Drain: one-by-one (simple, more sync overhead) vs batches (drain up to N — amortizes locks, better cache). Channel<T> implements all of it: CreateBounded(capacity, new BoundedChannelOptions { FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait }) plus TryWrite/WaitToWriteAsync, ReadAllAsync with cancellation, and ChannelClosedException semantics on Complete(). Legacy alternative: BlockingCollection<T>(new ConcurrentQueue<T>(), bound) with Add/Take/CompleteAdding — blocking-only, fine for thread-based workers. Metrics: current depth (gauge), dropped count (counter), consumer lag — alert on sustained full. Poison messages: try/catch per item so one bad payload doesn't kill the consumer; dead-letter after N retries.
internalWorking: Bounded channels combine a ConcurrentQueue with async waiter lists and a completion flag; WaitToWriteAsync parks the producer as a Task (no thread) until space frees. FullMode.Wait applies backpressure; Drop* modes keep a dropped counter. BlockingCollection wraps any IProducerConsumerCollection with semaphores (Add/Take block kernel-side).
realWorldUsage: Log shippers, ingestion buffers, socket read→parse→handle pipelines, background email/SMS senders, and telemetry aggregation.
commonMistake: Unbounded Channel (default!) under bursty load, blocking Take on async code (thread-pool starvation — use async reads), no poison-message handling (one bad item loops forever), and missing Complete() (consumers hang at shutdown).
technicalConversation: Ask what happens at 3am when the downstream API slows 10x — the answer should walk bound → policy → metrics → alert, not just 'it queues up'.
interviewFollowUp: When would you choose DropOldest over Wait, and what business conversation does that require?
keyTakeaway: Bound everything, pick an overflow policy deliberately, drain in batches, meter depth. Channels encode the whole design.

questionText: How does ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, TValue> differ from locking a Dictionary, and what are GetOrAdd/AddOrUpdate pitfalls?
shortAnswer: ConcurrentDictionary uses lock striping (many fine-grained locks) for scalable concurrent access; a locked Dictionary serializes everything on one lock. Pitfall: value factories in GetOrAdd/AddOrUpdate may execute multiple times — factories must be side-effect-free, with Lazy<T> for once-only init.
detailedAnswer: Dictionary + lock is correct but single-lane: every read and write serializes, killing scalability at ~4+ cores under contention. ConcurrentDictionary stripes locks across buckets (plus lock-free reads in the modern implementation), so disjoint keys proceed in parallel — dramatically higher throughput for caches and counters. API notes: GetOrAdd(key, factory) returns existing or adds — but the factory can run concurrently on multiple threads with only one winner kept, so factories must be pure (no DB writes, no increments); for expensive once-only values store Lazy<T> (publication-only or execution-and-publication modes). AddOrUpdate(key, addFactory, (k, old) => new) similarly may retry the update function — keep it pure and cheap. Count/IsEmpty are O(n)-ish snapshots (locks all stripes — avoid in hot paths; use IsEmpty for emptiness). Enumeration is a moment-in-time snapshot (safe, possibly stale). GetOrAdd with a direct value (not factory) still works but always evaluates the argument — pass factories for expensive construction. Atomic patterns: counters via AddOrUpdate(key, 1, (k, v) => v + 1) — correct under contention, unlike read-modify-write on a plain Dictionary even with coarse locking subtleties. For sets, ConcurrentDictionary<T, byte> fills the missing ConcurrentHashSet role.
internalWorking: Buckets carry individual locks (lock objects per bucket group); reads use volatile loads with no lock in the fast path. Tables grow by rehashing under a global growth lock while reads continue. Value-factory races are inherent to the lock-free-ish design — documented, by design, caller-managed.
realWorldUsage: Caches, dedup registries, per-key locks (dictionary of SemaphoreSlim), counters, and connection/session tables in servers.
commonMistake: Side-effecting factories (double DB inserts), ContainsKey-then-Add races (use GetOrAdd), Count in loops (expensive snapshot), and storing Lazy without .Value discipline (Lazy<Lazy<T>> nests when factories return Lazy).
technicalConversation: Ask how they would prove a double-init bug — intermittent duplicate rows despite GetOrAdd is the production symptom; the fix conversation is Lazy publication modes.
interviewFollowUp: Why is Lazy<T> with ExecutionAndPublication the standard companion for expensive cached values?
keyTakeaway: Striped locks scale; factories must be pure. Lazy<T> for once-only, AddOrUpdate for atomic counters.

questionText: When should you use ConcurrentQueue, ConcurrentStack, or ConcurrentBag, and what are their trade-offs?
shortAnswer: ConcurrentQueue<T> for multi-producer/consumer FIFO pipelines (the default choice); ConcurrentStack<T> for LIFO with lowest contention; ConcurrentBag<T> for unordered object pools with thread affinity. All are lock-free-ish and enumerable-as-snapshot; none supports blocking takes (pair with events/channels) or bounded capacity.
detailedAnswer: ConcurrentQueue<T> (Michael-Scott segments): Enqueue/TryDequeue are wait-free-ish, ordering is FIFO per segment with segment-local staggering under contention (global FIFO holds logically; extreme contention may briefly reorder visibility — acceptable for work items, not for strict sequencing). ConcurrentStack<T> (Treiber stack): Push/TryPop contend on one head — lowest overhead single-producer, hottest contention multi-producer; TryPopRange pops batches efficiently. ConcurrentBag<T> (work-stealing lists): per-thread storage gives near-zero contention for same-thread produce/consume (object pools!), but cross-thread steals and unordered enumeration; Count is expensive (sums all lists). None block: polling TryDequeue burns CPU — use BlockingCollection wrappers or channels for take-semantics. None bound capacity — enforce bounds externally or use channels. Snapshots: ToArray/ToList and enumeration capture a moment (safe, O(n), possibly stale). Choices: pipelines → ConcurrentQueue; pools → ConcurrentBag (or ArrayPool for buffers); LIFO recursion offload → ConcurrentStack; async + backpressure + completion → Channel<T> (superset, usually the better answer in new code).
internalWorking: Queue: linked segments of 32-item slots with per-segment head/tail (CAS updates). Stack: single head pointer CAS (fast, contended). Bag: ThreadLocal WorkStealingQueue + global queue; local push/pop are plain list ops, steals take the global lock briefly.
realWorldUsage: Task schedulers (queues), connection/buffer pools (bags), parallel aggregation collectors (bags/queues drained at the end), and DFS worklists (stacks).
commonMistake: Polling loops on TryDequeue (100% CPU — block or await instead), relying on cross-thread FIFO exactness, Count-based control flow (expensive + instantly stale), and ConcurrentBag for ordered data (it explicitly does not order).
technicalConversation: Ask when they would still pick BlockingCollection over Channel — existing thread-based worker code with Take() semantics is the honest legacy answer; new code should prefer channels.
interviewFollowUp: Why does ConcurrentBag outperform ConcurrentQueue for same-thread pool reuse, and when does it lose?
keyTakeaway: Queue for pipelines, Bag for pools, Stack for LIFO. No blocking, no bounds, no exact cross-thread order — channels cover those.

questionText: How does BlockingCollection<T> work, and when is Channel<T> the better choice?
shortAnswer: BlockingCollection<T> adds bounding + blocking take/complete semantics over any IProducerConsumerCollection (default ConcurrentQueue). Use it for classic thread-based producer/consumer. Prefer Channel<T> for async code: true async waits, backpressure modes, cancellation, and completion without burning threads.
detailedAnswer: BlockingCollection constructor takes the inner collection + optional bound: new BlockingCollection<Job>(new ConcurrentQueue<Job>(), 100). Producers Add (blocks when full) / TryAdd with timeout; consumers Take (blocks when empty) / TryTake / GetConsumingEnumerable() (foreach that ends on CompleteAdding — the graceful-shutdown pattern). CompleteAdding + IsCompleted coordinate drain-then-exit. It shines with dedicated long-running consumer threads (TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning) and legacy sync code. Channel<T> supersedes it for async: WriteAsync/ReadAsync truly park (no thread), BoundedChannelFullMode gives Wait/DropNewest/DropOldest/DropWrite policies (vs single blocking behavior), Reader.Completion is an awaitable Task (vs IsCompleted polling), and cancellation tokens flow through every call. Migration is mechanical: GetConsumingEnumerable → await foreach ReadAllAsync(ct); Add → WriteAsync; CompleteAdding → Writer.Complete(). Keep BlockingCollection when consumers must be synchronous threads (P/Invoke callbacks, STA/COM pumps) or when the codebase is thread-based end to end. Never mix: blocking Take inside async methods starves the pool (sync-over-async); async reads inside thread workers add needless machinery.
internalWorking: BlockingCollection pairs the inner collection with two SemaphoreSlims (free slots, available items); Add/Take wait kernel-side. Channels use lock-free queues plus async waiter op-lists; WaitToReadAsync returns incomplete Tasks completed by writers — zero threads while idle.
realWorldUsage: Legacy worker services, file watchers feeding processors, serial-port readers, and any thread-per-consumer design predating async.
commonMistake: Blocking Take in async handlers (pool starvation under load), forgetting CompleteAdding (consumers hang forever at shutdown), unbounded default (BlockingCollection() without bound grows until OOM), and catching OperationCanceledException as failure (it is normal shutdown — handle explicitly).
technicalConversation: Ask how their consumers shut down cleanly today — CompleteAdding/Completion discipline (drain-then-exit, no lost items, no hangs) separates production code from demos.
interviewFollowUp: What is the async equivalent of GetConsumingEnumerable, and how does cancellation propagate?
keyTakeaway: BlockingCollection = sync threads + bounds + completion. Channels = the async superset. Never block-take in async code.

questionText: How do Interlocked, lock, and concurrent collections compare for shared counters and flags?
shortAnswer: Interlocked for single-variable atomics (counters, flags) — fastest, lock-free. lock for multi-step invariants across several fields. Concurrent collections for shared data structures. volatile/Volatile only for visibility, never for read-modify-write.
detailedAnswer: Interlocked.Increment/Decrement/Add/Exchange/CompareExchange compile to LOCK-prefixed CPU instructions (or CAS loops): atomic, full-fence, ~tens of nanoseconds, no context switch. Counters, sequence IDs, once-flags (Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref started, 1, 0) == 0), and lock-free state machines belong here. lock (Monitor) serializes critical sections: needed when an invariant spans multiple variables (transfer between accounts: debit A + credit B atomically) or wraps non-atomic structures. Keep sections tiny, never call unknown code (events, virtuals, plugins) inside — reentrancy + ordering deadlocks live there; always lock a private readonly object (never this/string/Type). SpinLock/SpinWait suit microsecond-held, uncontended paths (with backoff + yield fallback). volatile guarantees fresh reads/writes (no caching/reordering) but i++ is still three ops — a race; Volatile.Read/Write are explicit equivalents. MemoryBarrier/Thread.MemoryBarrier: full fences for hand-rolled protocols (rarely needed — prefer Interlocked). False sharing: adjacent counters on different cores ping-pong cache lines (64B) — pad hot counters ([StructLayout] or Padding structs) in extreme cases. Measure: lock convoy shows as thread-time in profilers; Interlocked contention as CAS-retry cycles.
internalWorking: Interlocked maps to XADD/CMPXCHG with LOCK (bus lock/cache-line reservation + implicit full memory fence). Monitor is a hybrid thin-lock (spin briefly, then kernel event wait) with ownership + recursion count. volatile inserts acquire/release half-fences (or no-op on x86 reads, fence on writes) — visibility without atomicity.
realWorldUsage: Metrics counters, id generators, connection-reference counts, lazy-init flags, and pool cursors (Interlocked); account transfers and cache-put-if-absent composites (lock); everything structural (concurrent collections).
commonMistake: volatile counter++ (still racy), lock(this) (external code can deadlock you), locking on strings/Type (process-wide shared!), long critical sections with I/O inside (convoy), and Double-checked locking without volatile/Interlocked (publish half-built objects).
technicalConversation: Ask them to make a counter correct three ways (Interlocked/lock/concurrent) and state when each wins — the trade-off vocabulary (atomicity scope vs contention vs overhead) is the senior signal.
interviewFollowUp: Why is double-checked locking broken without proper publication, and what is the modern alternative?
keyTakeaway: Interlocked = single-variable atomicity, lock = multi-field invariants, volatile = visibility only. Smallest scope that is correct.

questionText: What is false sharing, and how do you detect and fix it in hot concurrent code?
shortAnswer: False sharing is when independent variables share a 64-byte cache line, so cores invalidate each other's caches on every write — no logical race, but performance collapses. Detect via scaling collapse + coherence traffic; fix by padding hot fields to separate lines.
detailedAnswer: CPUs move memory in 64-byte cache lines with MESI coherence: a write by core A invalidates the line on core B, forcing a ~100ns+ refetch — even if A and B touch different variables that merely share the line. Classic shape: counters[threadId]++ in a tight parallel loop, or adjacent fields mutated by different threads (producer/consumer cursors). Symptoms: code scales to 2–4 cores then flatlines or regresses, with cache-coherence (not lock) dominating profiles; perf counters show high HITM (hit-modified) / remote-line traffic. Fixes: pad to 64B boundaries ([StructLayout(LayoutKind.Explicit)] with FieldOffset 0/64, or Padding structs / PaddedLong patterns), partition work so each core owns whole lines (chunked ranges, not interleaved indices), use per-core locals aggregated at the end (Parallel.For localFinally), or interlocked-on-separated slots. .NET specifics: object headers + method table consume the first 16 bytes of a line — account for them; arrays of structs pack tightly (good for locality, bad for per-core mutation — pad or privatize); ThreadLocal<T> + final merge sidesteps sharing entirely. Verify with BenchmarkDotNet thread-count scaling + hardware counters (or simply: does padding restore linear scaling?).
internalWorking: MESI: a store needs the line Exclusive; other copies Invalidate. Ping-ponging a line costs a last-level-cache/memory round trip per write (~40–100ns vs ~1ns L1). Padding wastes memory to buy coherence silence; the JIT lays out sequential structs tightly, so explicit layout is required to force separation.
realWorldUsage: Parallel aggregators, disruptor-style ring buffers (padded cursors are the pattern's core), socket buffer pools per core, and metrics recorders on hot paths.
commonMistake: Interleaved parallel writes to adjacent array slots, per-thread state in one shared object, 'fixing' with locks (adds overhead without removing coherence traffic — padding/privatization is the cure), and padding on cold paths (waste without benefit — profile first).
technicalConversation: Ask how they would distinguish lock contention from false sharing in a profile — lock waits show thread-time/blocking; coherence shows as cache-miss/HITM with no blocking, and padding is the experiment that confirms.
interviewFollowUp: Why does the disruptor pattern pad its sequence cursors, and what breaks if you remove the padding?
keyTakeaway: Shared lines, separate variables, collapsed scaling. Pad hot fields, privatize per core, verify by scaling.
